course-01.summary: Learn to think like a programmer before you learn a programming language: break problems into pieces, write steps a computer can't misread, use loops and decisions, hunt down bugs, and compare algorithms by counting their steps.
course-01.description: This course teaches the thinking behind every programming language, using everyday problems: sharing computers fairly at a community center, steering a delivery robot around a room, printing hundreds of name labels, deciding whether a library book can be borrowed, and finding a name in a list. About half the work happens on paper, with unplugged puzzles like robots on a grid, scrambled recipes, and a deck of cards. The other half happens in Scratch 3, MIT's free block-based editor, where your algorithms run for real: you build a fair-share calculator, a delivery robot, pen drawings made with loops, a library kiosk, a buggy alarm clock to fix, and a number-guessing robot that uses binary search. Step-through animations show the same algorithms written in Python, so you can watch the computer follow each step and see its variables change, without needing to learn Python. Each module has a Notes lesson, a Build-along, and a Practice set with hints and worked solutions, and the course ends with an algorithm of your own that you design, test, and explain.
course-01.audience: Absolute beginners, roughly ages 10 to 14, who have never written code and want a strong problem-solving foundation before choosing a programming language.
prerequisites: None. If you can follow a recipe and use a mouse, you're ready.
outcomes: Describe any problem by its goal, inputs, constraints, and output, and decompose it into pieces small enough to solve.
Write exact, ordered algorithms in plain English, as flowcharts, and as Scratch scripts, and track their state step by step.
Spot repeated steps and replace them with counting or condition-controlled loops, including loops inside loops.
Plan decisions with if/else and combined conditions, and test the edge cases where rules break.
Find and fix bugs by predicting, tracing by hand, and comparing expected results with actual ones.
Compare two correct algorithms, such as linear and binary search, by counting the steps each one takes.

course-02.summary: Design and build real games in Scratch, from a two-player race and an underwater catch game to a platformer, a clone-powered shooter, and a multi-level game of your own.
course-02.description: A self-paced game-design course in Scratch 3, the free block-based editor from the Scratch Foundation. You start by placing sprites on the stage's x–y grid and wiring scripts to events, then build a firefly scene, a key-mash race with a fair start and a referee that runs on broadcasts and a state variable, and Reef Catch, a catch game with easing, animation, sound, and visual feedback. Later modules add collisions, gravity, and jumping in a platformer, then clones, custom blocks (including run without screen refresh), and lists in a lane shooter that grows waves, a story, and difficulty that adapts to the player. Each module has Notes with quizzes, a step-by-step Build-along, and Practice exercises with hints and full solutions. The course ends with a capstone: a multi-level game you plan, build in milestones, playtest, and present.
course-02.audience: Beginners around ages 10 to 15 who want to make their own games, with no coding experience needed.
prerequisites: Comfortable using a mouse and keyboard and following multi-step instructions

Coordinate many sprites with broadcasts, variables, conditions, and a game state variable instead of fragile timers.

Build collisions, gravity, and jumping for a platformer.
Manage many objects with clones, reusable custom blocks, and lists.

course-03.summary: A self-paced first course in Python for teens who have never typed code: write real programs in Thonny, watch every value change as they run, and finish with a text app of your own.
course-03.description: You'll install Thonny, a free Python editor that comes with Python built in, and use its Variables panel and step-by-step debugger to see exactly what your code does. Each module teaches one idea in a Notes lesson, uses it to build one complete program (a text-adventure status tracker, a club sign-up slip that cleans up messy typing, a bike-share fare calculator, a mental math game, a race pace calculator, and a virtual pet), then sets fresh practice problems with hints and worked solutions. Every code example on the page has been run, so the output and error messages you see are the real ones. The course ends with a capstone: a text-based app you plan, build in milestones, and test yourself.

course-04.summary: Go from short Python exercises to real command-line tools: a grade book, a contacts manager, and a quiz that saves its scores, built with collections, small functions, JSON files, validation, and debugging.
course-04.description: This self-paced course picks up where basic Python leaves off and moves from one-file exercises to programs with several files and saved data. Learners set up VS Code with Microsoft's Python extension and a virtual environment, then build a grade book that turns messy text into a ranked report, a contacts manager made of small testable functions, and a quiz game that loads its questions from JSON and keeps a score history that survives crashes and damaged files. Later modules cover libraries and input validation, systematic debugging, and designing a complete command-line project, ending with a capstone: a flash-card, expense, or inventory tool that remembers its data and comes with tests. Code on the lesson pages runs for real and shows its actual output, and every module ends with practice exercises that have hints and worked solutions.

course-05.summary: Go from scripts full of parallel lists to Python programs built from small, well-named classes, and prove they work with pytest.
course-05.description: You will write every line in VS Code with Python 3 and pytest, starting with a bank account that replaces a tangle of parallel lists and growing it into a small library and inventory system. Along the way you model state with classes and methods, choose between composition and inheritance, protect interfaces with properties, express intent with dunder methods, dataclasses, and type hints, raise your own exceptions, split code into modules, and refactor with tests holding the behaviour steady. Every lesson pairs notes with diagrams, step-through traces of objects changing, and code that was really run, then a build-along and a practice set with worked solutions. The course ends with a capstone application you design, test, and explain.
course-05.audience: Students who already write Python functions and use lists and dicts, and now want their programs to stay understandable as they grow past a few hundred lines.

course-06.summary: Write web pages by hand with HTML and CSS: a profile site, a recipe page, a styled sign-up form, responsive layouts with Flexbox and Grid, and finally a multi-page website of your own.
course-06.description: You type every page yourself in VS Code, see it update the moment you save with the free Live Server extension, and look inside it with Chrome or Firefox DevTools. Every lesson shows code next to a live result, so you can see exactly what each tag and rule does. The course starts with how a browser turns a file into a page, then covers document structure, links, images and file paths, semantic landmarks, lists, tables, and accessible forms. Next come selectors, the cascade, specificity, and the box model, followed by Flexbox, Grid, responsive layouts, keyboard and screen reader access, typography, and sharing one stylesheet across several pages. Each module has a Notes lesson, a step-by-step build, and practice problems with hints and hidden solutions. The course ends with a capstone: a responsive multi-page website you plan, build, test, and publish.

Organize a project into folders and link files to each other with correct relative paths.
Predict which CSS rule wins using specificity and source order, and size elements precisely with the box model.

course-08.summary: Learn Git and GitHub the way teams use them: clear commits, branches, pull requests, issues, code review, merge conflicts, documentation, licenses, releases, and automated checks.
course-08.description: You'll version a real project from the first commit, then put it on GitHub and change it the way working developers do: plan each change as an issue, build it on a branch, open a pull request, review a partner's work with line comments and suggested changes, and merge. Later modules cover resolving merge conflicts without losing anyone's work, writing a README, choosing an open-source license, tagging releases with a changelog, and running automatic checks with GitHub Actions. Lessons show each command with the output it prints, and each idea is also shown in VS Code's Source Control view. The course uses Git, a free GitHub account, and VS Code, all free on Windows, macOS, and Chromebooks with Linux turned on.

course-09.summary: Build real inventions with the BBC micro:bit in free Microsoft MakeCode: a name badge, a reaction-time game, a step counter with a compass, radio messengers, and a sensor logger, all testable in the browser simulator.
course-09.description: You program the BBC micro:bit in Microsoft MakeCode, a free browser editor whose built-in simulator runs every program in the course, so no hardware is required. After a setup module, each core module pairs a notes lesson that teaches the ideas with a build-along that makes one working invention, then a set of practice problems with hints and full solutions. You start with buttons, the LED screen, and events, then read the accelerometer, compass, light, temperature, and microphone, send radio messages between boards, compare MakeCode with MicroPython, collect sensor data, and finish by designing, testing, and documenting a connected invention of your own. Programs are shown as MakeCode JavaScript that you can paste into the editor and view as blocks.
course-09.audience: Middle and high school beginners who have tried a little coding, in Scratch or any language, and want to make things that sense the world and react to it.

outcomes: Set up MakeCode, test programs in the simulator, and transfer them safely to a real micro:bit.
Program the LED screen, buttons, and touch logo using events, loops, and variables.
Turn noisy accelerometer, compass, light, temperature, and sound readings into reliable decisions.
Exchange radio messages between micro:bits and read the same program in MakeCode and MicroPython.
Collect and chart sensor data, then design, test, and document a connected invention.

course-10.summary: Build and debug real Arduino circuits in a free browser simulator, from your first blinking LED to sensors, motors, state machines, and a working robot.
course-10.description: Every circuit in this course runs on a simulated Arduino Uno in Wokwi, a free in-browser simulator, so you can wire LEDs, buttons, potentiometers, light and temperature sensors, servos, and motors without buying parts or risking damage. You write real Arduino C++ (the same code runs unchanged on a physical Uno), and you check the electrical math first with short Python programs that show their real output and charts on the page: Ohm's law, LED resistor sizing, voltage dividers, and ADC conversions. Each module has notes that teach the ideas, a build-along that makes one working project step by step, and a practice set with hints and full solutions. Later modules drive motors safely through a driver, organize robot behavior as state machines with feedback, test robots under changing conditions, and finish with an obstacle-avoiding or line-following robot capstone. Tinkercad Circuits works as a backup simulator, and an optional starter kit lets you build everything for real with Arduino IDE 2.
course-10.audience: Teens and beginners who have written a few programs with conditions and loops, and want to understand circuits, sensors, motors, and how robots make decisions.
prerequisites: Write simple programs with variables, if/else, and loops (in any language)
Comfortable using a web browser and copying text between windows
outcomes: Apply Ohm's law and power calculations to size resistors and keep circuits within safe current and heat limits.
Lay out breadboard circuits with LEDs, buttons, and potentiometers, and find wiring faults by tracing nodes.
Read digital and analog sensors, convert raw readings to volts and real units, and smooth noisy signals.
Drive servos and DC motors safely through a motor driver with a separate power supply.
Organize robot behavior as a state machine with feedback, and test it under varied conditions.
Build, test, and present a simulated or physical obstacle-avoiding or line-following robot.

course-11.summary: Build the server side of a web app in Python: read real HTTP traffic with curl, design REST endpoints and JSON contracts, write routes with FastAPI, store data in SQLite, protect and validate requests, and connect a web page to your own tested API.
course-11.description: This course follows one project from an empty folder to a working backend. You start by installing Python, VS Code, and FastAPI in a virtual environment, then run a server on your own laptop and poke it with curl and FastAPI's built-in /docs page. Next you read real requests and responses from GitHub's public API, learning methods, status codes, headers, query strings, and JSON by looking at actual traffic. You design a REST contract for a notes API on paper (endpoints, status codes, error shapes, pagination, versioning), then build it in FastAPI with Pydantic models and test it with FastAPI's TestClient. Later modules swap the in-memory list for a SQLite database using Python's built-in sqlite3 module and safe parameterized queries, add authentication basics and input validation, connect a browser front end with fetch, and finish with a capstone app you plan, build, test, and present. The runnable examples on these pages were run when each lesson was built, so the JSON you see is what FastAPI actually returned. Each module has a Notes lesson, a Build-along, and a Practice set with hints and worked solutions.
course-11.audience: Teens and early college students who already write Python (functions, lists, dictionaries, and a little about classes) and want to build the server and database behind web and mobile apps.
prerequisites: Python basics: functions, lists, dictionaries, loops, and reading a traceback
Comfort typing commands in a terminal, or willingness to learn it in Module 1
Some HTML and JavaScript helps for the later module that connects a web page, but isn't needed before then
outcomes: Read and write HTTP by hand: methods, URLs and query strings, headers, status codes, and JSON bodies, using curl -i against real APIs.
Design a REST contract for a resource, with consistent endpoints, status codes, error shapes, pagination, and a plan for versioning.
Build a FastAPI service with path and query parameters, Pydantic request and response models, and correct 201, 204, 404, and 422 responses.
Model related data in SQLite tables and query it from Python with parameterized SQL.
Protect actions so users can only change their own data, and validate every input at the boundary.
Ship a tested, documented, database-backed web app and explain how its pieces talk to each other.

primaryTool.name: Python 3 with FastAPI, in VS Code
primaryTool.description: FastAPI is a free, open-source Python framework for building web APIs. You write ordinary Python functions with type hints, and FastAPI turns them into HTTP endpoints that validate their input, return JSON, and document themselves on an interactive /docs page. It runs on Uvicorn, a small web server that installs with it, and its TestClient lets you send requests to your app from a test file without starting a server. VS Code is the editor, curl is the command-line client, and SQLite comes built into Python.
setupSteps: Install Python 3.11 or newer from python.org (on a Chromebook, turn on Linux and install python3 with apt).
Install VS Code and Microsoft's Python extension.
Make a folder called backend-course, open it in VS Code, and create a virtual environment with python -m venv .venv.
Activate the environment and run python -m pip install "fastapi[standard]" (keep the quotes).
Save a short main.py that creates a FastAPI app with one route, then run fastapi dev main.py.
Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs in your browser, or run curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/ in a second terminal.
primaryTool.verification: The terminal prints 'Server started at http://127.0.0.1:8000', the /docs page lists your route, and curl -i shows HTTP/1.1 200 OK followed by your JSON.

course-11.freeCompletionPromise: Every lesson can be completed for $0. Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, SQLite, VS Code, and curl are all free, and curl already ships with Windows 10 and 11, macOS, and most Linux systems. The public API examples use GitHub's API, which answers simple read requests without an account or key. Everything runs on your own computer, with no hosting or paid services.

course-12.summary: Build a complete 2D platformer in Unity 6 with C#: scenes and prefabs, keyboard movement, physics and collisions, a Cinemachine camera, animation, UI, sound, enemies, levels, saving, and a shareable build.
course-12.description: You build one 2D game from an empty Universal 2D project to a finished build, using the free Unity 6.3 LTS Editor installed through Unity Hub and C# scripts written in Visual Studio or VS Code. Early modules compose a level from GameObjects, components, and prefabs, script frame-rate-independent movement with the Input System package, and then switch to Rigidbody 2D physics with colliders, triggers, layers, a jump with a ground check, and a Cinemachine follow camera. Later modules make the game readable to players with Animator states, a TextMeshPro HUD, and sound effects, add enemies with state-based behavior and levels that teach one mechanic at a time, save progress between sessions, and export a build to share. Every script is a real MonoBehaviour written against Unity 6 APIs. Each module has a Notes lesson that explains the ideas with diagrams and videos, a Build-along that adds a working system to the game step by step, and a Practice set with hints and full solutions. The course ends with a capstone game of your own, planned, tested, and presented with a rubric.
course-12.audience: Students who already program a little (in Python, JavaScript, Java, or C#) and want to learn how real games are structured and built, from strong middle schoolers through early college.

A Windows 10/11 PC, a Mac on macOS 13 or newer, or an Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 computer with about 15 GB free (Chromebooks can't run the Unity Editor)
outcomes: Organize a game from scenes, GameObjects, components, and prefabs, and explain when Awake, Start, Update, and FixedUpdate run.
Write C# MonoBehaviour scripts that read the keyboard and mouse with the Input System and move objects at the same speed on any frame rate.
Build platformer physics with Rigidbody 2D, colliders, triggers, layers, a ground-checked jump, and a comfortable Cinemachine follow camera.
Give players clear feedback with sprite animation, an on-screen HUD, and sound.
Design enemy behavior and levels that teach, test, and then twist one mechanic.

course-13.summary: Load, clean, summarize, and chart real-world tables with pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib in free Google Colab notebooks, and learn to make claims your data can actually support.
course-13.description: This course turns Python you already know into a working data-science toolkit. Every lesson runs in Google Colab, a free notebook in the browser with pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, and seaborn already installed, so you see real tables and real charts from the first lesson. You'll inspect CSV and JSON exports and catch the text hiding in number columns, replace slow loops with vectorized NumPy and pandas code, summarize and join tables with groupby and merge, and clean messy observations step by step: disguised missing values, duplicates, mixed units, misspelled categories, and impossible readings. Later modules cover summary statistics and honest, accessible charts, the limits of correlation and the ways samples mislead, and notebooks that anyone can rerun from top to bottom. The datasets are small and realistic: survey exports, bike-share trips, weather stations, air sensors, and a street-tree survey. Each core module has a Notes lesson with runnable examples, a Build-along that makes one real analysis, and a Practice set with hints and full solutions, and the course ends with a reproducible investigation of a dataset you choose.
course-13.audience: Middle and high school students, and early college learners, who can already write basic Python (variables, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions) and want to answer real questions with data.
prerequisites: Basic Python: variables, lists, dictionaries, loops, if statements, and functions.
Comfort reading a short error message and trying a fix.
No statistics or prior pandas experience needed.
outcomes: Load CSV and JSON data into pandas and check shapes, types, and missing values before trusting any number.
Write vectorized NumPy and pandas code with boolean masks, loc and iloc, new columns, groupby, and merge.
Clean messy data step by step (missing markers, duplicates, units, inconsistent categories, impossible values) and log every decision.
Summarize data with the right statistics and draw clear, accessible Matplotlib charts.

course-14.summary: Find out what AI and machine learning can and can't do by training real models in your browser with Google's Teachable Machine, then learn to judge their scores, their fairness, their use of personal data, and whether AI belongs in a problem at all.
course-14.description: This is a no-coding course about how machine learning actually works and how to think clearly about it. You'll train real models in Teachable Machine, Google's free in-browser tool: a thumbs-up detector, a clap-and-snap sound classifier, and a recycling sorter that you deliberately break and fix by changing only its examples. You'll tell rules from learned models, name the task a system does (classification, regression, clustering, recommendation, or generation), and find out what chatbots are really doing when they answer. You'll describe data as features and labels, see decision boundaries drawn on charts, hold out test data, catch overfitting and leaks, and watch a neural network learn inside TensorFlow Playground. Later modules cover confidence scores and bias, privacy and consent, deepfakes and checking AI-made claims, and deciding when AI is the wrong tool. Charts in the lessons are drawn by short Python programs that run for you, so you read the picture, not the code; Google Colab is an optional extra for the curious. Modules 2 to 7 each have a Notes lesson, a hands-on Build-along, and a Practice set of judgement problems with worked solutions, and the course ends with a written recommendation on whether and how to use AI for a proposed project.
course-14.audience: Curious beginners, roughly ages 12 and up, plus teachers and parents, who want to understand AI well enough to use it, question it, and explain it, before or instead of learning to program it.
prerequisites: None. No coding, math beyond percentages, or AI experience needed.
A laptop or desktop computer with Chrome or Firefox. A webcam and microphone help but aren't required.
outcomes: Tell a rule-based system from a machine learning model, and name the task family of any AI product from the kind of answer it gives.
Describe a dataset as examples, features, and labels, and spot features that leak the answer or won't exist at prediction time.
Train, test, and improve image and sound models in Teachable Machine by changing their examples, and catch shortcuts a model has learned.
Explain why models are scored on held-out test data, recognize overfitting on a chart, and describe how a neural network learns by nudging its weights.
Interpret confidence scores, check whether errors fall unevenly on different groups, and plan data collection that respects privacy and consent.
Decide whether AI fits a proposed problem, and write a recommendation that weighs data, risks, oversight, and simpler alternatives.

course-15.summary: Train your own image, sound, and pose models in the browser with Google's Teachable Machine, no code required, and learn to collect fair data, read confidence honestly, test on examples the model has never seen, and fix the mistakes you find.
course-15.description: A hands-on, no-code machine learning course built on Teachable Machine, Google's free browser tool for training image, audio, and pose models. You start with a two-class model in five minutes, then build a rock, paper, scissors recognizer the careful way: a written data plan, classes a single camera frame can tell apart, examples recorded in rounds across lighting, distance, and both hands, and only people who agreed to be in the data. You balance the classes and watch what a ten-to-one imbalance does, read the accuracy and loss graphs under the hood, and learn what epochs, batch size, and learning rate control. Then you test properly: a folder of photos from new rooms, light, and people that never goes into training, a test sheet with every answer's confidence, and a recycling sorter tested on objects held out from the start. Later modules turn test results into confusion matrices, separate false positives from false negatives, repair weak data with targeted examples, export a model with the labels and limits someone else needs, and connect its predictions to an interactive project. Charts and step-through animations explain what the model is doing; you never have to write code. Each core module has Notes with quizzes, a step-by-step Build-along, and Practice experiments with expected results, and the course ends with a prototype of your own.
course-15.audience: Beginners, roughly ages 12 to 18, who know what AI is and want to build and test real models without programming.

course-16.summary: Train your first machine-learning models in Python with scikit-learn: turn tables into features and targets, split and preprocess data without fooling yourself, and compare k-nearest neighbors, linear and logistic regression, and decision trees using the right metrics.
course-16.description: This course is for Python programmers meeting machine learning for the first time. Everything runs in Google Colab, a free notebook in the browser with scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, and matplotlib already installed, so a school Chromebook works as well as any laptop. You train a model on the classic iris flowers in the first module, then learn the workflow behind it: choosing features and a target, spotting columns that leak the answer, splitting off a test set with train_test_split and stratify, and scaling and one-hot encoding data inside a pipeline. Next you open up two models completely, building k-nearest neighbors by hand and writing gradient descent from scratch to fit a line, then checking both against scikit-learn. Later modules add logistic regression and decision trees, the metrics that tell you whether a model is good enough (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and confusion matrices), and how to diagnose overfitting and compare models fairly. A capstone pulls it together into a documented comparison of several models on one dataset. course-17.summary: Wire and program a Raspberry Pi Pico W in a free browser simulator, then grow it into a connected sensor station: read sensors, drive LEDs and servos, log and smooth time-series data, publish it over MQTT to a dashboard, and lock down remote control.
course-17.description: Every circuit in this course runs on a simulated Raspberry Pi Pico W in Wokwi, a free in-browser simulator, so you can wire buttons, potentiometers, temperature and light sensors, LEDs, and servos without buying parts. You write real MicroPython (machine.Pin, machine.ADC, machine.PWM, network.WLAN), the same code a physical Pico W runs, and the simulated board joins a virtual Wi-Fi network called Wokwi-GUEST to reach the internet. Data work happens in regular Python cells that run right on the lesson page: parsing CSV logs, smoothing noisy readings, spotting gaps, and drawing charts with matplotlib. Along the way you learn the Linux terminal (the same commands work on a Raspberry Pi, a Mac, WSL on Windows, or a Chromebook's Linux environment), GPIO numbering, and the electrical rules that keep real pins alive. Later modules send readings as JSON over MQTT, build a live dashboard, authenticate devices before they can act on commands, keep passwords out of source code, and plan for sensor, network, and dashboard failures. Each module has notes that teach the ideas, a build-along that makes one working project, and a practice set with hints and full solutions. course-18.summary: Build machine learning models small enough to run on a microcontroller: slice sensor streams into windows, extract features with NumPy, train tiny classifiers, quantize them to int8 by hand, and plan a deployment that fits real limits on memory, latency, power, and privacy.
course-18.description: TinyML is machine learning on chips with kilobytes of memory, like the ones inside fitness bands, smart speakers, and wildlife sensors. This course teaches it the way an engineer meets it: as a set of trade-offs you can measure. You start by deciding when a model should run on the device and when it should run in the cloud, using latency, bandwidth, privacy, power, cost, and connectivity numbers you calculate yourself. Then you work in Google Colab with NumPy, scikit-learn, and PyTorch to turn a raw accelerometer stream into labeled windows, compute features such as RMS and FFT peaks, train small classifiers, and check them without data leakage. You build spectrograms and MFCCs from audio, train a keyword spotter, and quantize its weights from float32 to int8 with your own scale and zero-point code, measuring the size and accuracy before and after. Later modules budget RAM, flash, and response time, plan a deployment and test it against real-world accuracy, and trade battery life against privacy with duty cycles and on-device decisions. Edge Impulse Studio, on its free Developer plan, shows the same pipeline in a production tool, with your phone working as a free sensor. Every Python example on these pages runs for real when the lesson is built, so the charts and numbers you see are real outputs. Each core module has a Notes lesson, a Build-along, and a Practice set with hints and worked solutions, and the course ends with a capstone device plan.

course-19.summary: Learn to compare machine learning models in a way that survives scrutiny: feature engineering inside scikit-learn pipelines, the right cross-validation for your data, tuning on a compute budget, class imbalance, ensembles, leakage hunting, calibration, interpretation, and error analysis by slice.
course-19.description: Most model comparisons fall apart under one good question: was the test data really unseen, would the ranking survive a different split, is the probability of 0.8 really 80%? This course teaches the habits that make the answer yes. You work in Google Colab with scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, and matplotlib. Early modules put every feature-engineering step inside a Pipeline and ColumnTransformer (including FunctionTransformer and transformer classes you write yourself), then measure performance with KFold, StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit, and nested cross-validation, and tune with grid, randomized, and successive-halving searches plus early stopping, all sized to finish in seconds. Later modules handle rare classes, compare forests and gradient boosting, hunt down leakage, check whether predicted probabilities are calibrated, explain what a model relies on, and find the slices of data where it fails. Every example uses data that ships with scikit-learn or is generated in the notebook, and every Python cell on these pages was run to produce the numbers and charts you see. Each core module has a Notes lesson, a Build-along, and a Practice set with hints and worked solutions. The course ends with a capstone: a reproducible model-comparison report with a recommendation and its limitations.

course-21.summary: Learn how language models read text by building the pieces yourself: tokenizers, word vectors, similarity search, text classifiers, entity extractors, attention, and finally a grounded document question-answering system with citations and an evaluation harness.

You'll normalize and tokenize text, train a byte-pair-encoding tokenizer from scratch, learn word vectors from co-occurrence counts, and compare one-hot, count, TF-IDF, and embedding representations. Then you'll rank documents by cosine similarity, train naive Bayes and logistic regression classifiers on realistic support tickets, and evaluate them honestly with confusion matrices, cross-validation, and confidence thresholds. Module 4 opens up a real transformer: you'll run a named-entity model from the Hugging Face Hub, combine it with regex rules, and follow a sentence from tokens to ids to logits, then chart its attention heads. Later modules cover attention and context budgets, prompts with structured outputs and validation, retrieval-augmented generation with citations, hallucination checks, the choice between retrieval and fine-tuning, and evaluation before deployment. You work in Google Colab with scikit-learn, NumPy, matplotlib, and Hugging Face transformers. Code that runs on the lesson pages uses small datasets typed into the cell, and the output you see came from actually running it; cells that download models are marked to run in Colab, with their real output shown. course-22.summary: Use machine learning as a careful scientific instrument: frame questions that can come out wrong, read papers like a referee, audit datasets for provenance and batch effects, beat simple baselines, put intervals on every number, test for leakage, and reproduce a published result.
course-22.description: Many published ML results in science don't survive a second look: a test set from the same hospital as the training data, a deep network that a two-parameter logistic regression matches, a 2-point gain measured on 60 images. This course teaches the habits that catch those problems before your own project makes them. You work in Google Colab (or Jupyter) with NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, and matplotlib. You start by setting up a project that can be rerun: a folder that keeps raw data raw, pinned library versions, seeds, data fingerprints, and run records. Then you turn hunches into testable questions, build an evidence table that recomputes what papers left out, audit multi-site datasets for missingness, batch effects, and confounding, design randomized and blocked follow-up experiments sized with a power analysis, and climb a baseline ladder from dummy models to linear models before anything complex. Later modules quantify uncertainty with confidence and bootstrap intervals, run ablations, sensitivity checks, and leakage hunts, and practice reproducing and reporting results honestly, including discrepancies. Real cases from the literature, such as the pneumonia model that learned to recognize hospitals and Kapoor and Narayanan's survey of leakage across 30 fields, appear throughout. Every example uses simulated scientific data with realistic structure (sites, batches, repeated measurements) or datasets that ship with scikit-learn, and every Python cell on these pages was run to produce the numbers and charts you see. Each core module has a Notes lesson, a Build-along, and a Practice set with worked solutions, and the course ends with a reproduction study of a published result.

course-25.summary: Build your own agent harness in plain Python: a runtime loop with validated tools, a subprocess sandbox with timeouts and output limits, retries that know when to give up, JSONL traces you can replay, eval sets with deterministic and model-based graders, and then specialized agents with routing, loop controls, approvals, rollback, and adversarial tests.
course-25.description: Frameworks hide the parts of an agent that decide whether it is safe and whether it works. In this course you write those parts yourself, as one Python package called harness that grows module by module in a project folder called harness-lab. You start with a single model interface, complete(messages, tools), that both a scripted fake model and a real client implement; the real client speaks the OpenAI-compatible chat API, so it works with a free local model through Ollama or with a hosted provider. Then you build the runtime loop (message history, a tool registry with JSON Schema validation, structured errors, stop rules, and a verify step), run model-written code in a child process with a time limit, an output cap, and a stripped environment, and learn exactly what that does not protect against and when you need a container or VM instead. You record every model call and tool call as JSONL traces with tokens and latency, replay runs for free, and turn traces into versioned eval cases with graders. Later modules attack your own graders, measure success rate, latency, tokens, and cost, route work across planner, worker, and reviewer agents, and add loop limits, human approvals, and rollback before anything reaches a repository. The harness uses only the Python standard library, and every runnable cell on these pages uses the scripted model, so the code you see ran offline to produce the output shown. Each core module has a Notes lesson, a Build-along, and a Practice set with hints and worked solutions, and the course ends with a capstone: a secure, evaluated multi-agent system you attack and improve.
